articles.title: A Tennessee UPS driver kept working after a 2022 rear-end crash but said his shoulder injury threatened his future earnings; a November 9 appeals court upheld a $575,000 jury award against the other driver and employer
articles.summary: A Tennessee appeals court has upheld a $575,000 compensation award to a UPS driver injured in a 2022 collision.
articles.body: A Tennessee appeals court has upheld a $575,000 compensation award to a UPS driver injured in a 2022 collision. The court ruled on November 9 that the evidence supported the jury's findings that the crash caused permanent shoulder damage and affected the driver's future earning capacity.The case involved Randy Gooden, whose vehicle was hit from behind by Bryant Johnson on January 13, 2022. Johnson worked for Serra Chevrolet LLC. Gooden sued both, seeking $1.5 million in damages.According to the judgement, Gooden returned to his UPS delivery job but said shoulder pain made his work difficult. He sometimes needed customers to help him complete his duties and was unsure whether he could continue working until the age of 52 or 53, as he had planned.A jury found Johnson and Serra Chevrolet fully responsible for the accident and awarded Gooden $575,000 after a trial in February 2025. The defendants challenged the verdict, but the trial court rejected their request to overturn or reduce it. They then appealed.Medical evidence and conflicting opinionsGooden sought treatment soon after the crash for back and right shoulder pain. Physiotherapy began on January 31, 2022. The assessment found limited shoulder movement and reduced grip strength in his right hand.Orthopaedic surgeon Dr Apurva Dalal began treating him in February. He diagnosed rotator cuff inflammation, shoulder impingement, arthritis and small partial tears in the rotator cuff. Treatment included medication, a steroid injection and physiotherapy.Although Gooden's movement improved, he continued to report pain and difficulty sleeping, lifting, pushing and pulling. Dalal allowed him to return to work without restrictions in May 2022. At a June appointment, Gooden said his shoulder sometimes locked, but the doctor found full movement during the examination.When Dalal examined him again in September, he found reduced shoulder mobility. He said the earlier improvement may have followed the steroid injection, which temporarily reduced inflammation. A congenital shoulder condition could also have contributed to the deterioration.Dalal could not identify the exact reason for the change but maintained that the collision had caused a permanent injury. He advised Gooden to avoid repetitive shoulder movements, strenuous overhead activity and lifting more than 25 pounds. Surgery remained an option if physiotherapy failed, though it was not guaranteed to help.The defence's medical expert, Dr Claiborne Christian, agreed that Gooden had shoulder impingement and that a collision could cause it. However, he believed the accident-related injuries had resolved by June 2022 and attributed the continuing problems to pre-existing conditions. Christian had reviewed the medical records but had not examined Gooden.Dispute over future earningsGooden told the trial that he continued working because he needed to support his family. He did not disclose his medical restrictions to UPS because he feared losing his job.Dr David Strauser, a rehabilitation psychology expert, estimated that Gooden could lose $74,000 to $84,000 in annual earning capacity if he could no longer work as a UPS driver or needed surgery. Gooden earned between $105,000 and $115,000 a year, including overtime, while another delivery job could pay about $30,000.Strauser said people who continue physically demanding work beyond medical restrictions may be unable to sustain it after five or six years.The defendants questioned this estimate, pointing out that Gooden had not suffered a wage reduction and UPS had not indicated that it planned to end his employment. There was also no medical evidence that surgery would be necessary. They further cited a medical form Gooden completed in April 2023, in which he listed high blood pressure as his only physical ailment and did not report shoulder, arm, neck or back limitations.Court upholds jury's decisionThe appeals court found sufficient evidence to support the jury's findings on permanent injury and future earning capacity. It said the jury was entitled to accept Dalal's opinion despite the defence expert's different assessment.The court also rejected the argument that Gooden could not be compensated for future lost earnings because he was still employed. It considered his evidence that he was working beyond the doctor's restrictions and Strauser's assessment of how long he might be able to continue.The jury could reasonably conclude that Gooden might lose two to four years of the employment he had expected to continue. The court found that the $225,000 awarded for lost earning capacity was within a reasonable range.The total award included $250,000 for permanent injury, $225,000 for lost earning capacity, $40,000 each for past and future pain and suffering, and $10,000 each for past and future loss of enjoyment of life.The appeals court affirmed the Shelby County Circuit Court's judgment and remanded the case for any further proceedings required.You use AI every day. articles.title: A Texas boy has lived with foster parents since he was weeks old after his mother gave birth while imprisoned; a November 10 appeals ruling upheld the termination of her parental rights as the couple seeks adoption
articles.summary: The people who take a child into their home, look after him and are a constant presence in his growing years may form his earliest memories.
articles.body: The people who take a child into their home, look after him and are a constant presence in his growing years may form his earliest memories. For one Texas boy, that family life began just weeks after he was born when he was placed with foster parents while his biological mother was in jail. More than four years later, a legal battle over his future reached an appellate court, which upheld a ruling to terminate his mother’s parental rights. Nov. 10, 2026: The Texas Fourteenth Court of Appeals ruled to allow the foster parents’ efforts to seek adoption to go forward.A childhood in foster familyLiam, as the child is referred to in the proceedings, was born on March 10, 2022, while his mother was in prison, the Texas Fourteenth Court of Appeals said. He went to live with his foster parents in April that year and has been in their care ever since.According to the court file, the mother had signed a temporary placement agreement allowing the Loving Houston Adoption Agency to place the infant in foster care. Crucially, the Texas Department of Family and Protective Services was not a party to the proceedings which ultimately resulted in the termination case.In October 2022, the foster parents filed a lawsuit to terminate the mother’s parental rights. Later, they amended their petition to adopt, demonstrating their desire to give Liam a permanent family environment.Mother challenges the legal standing of the foster parentsEventually the case went to trial and the district court in Fort Bend County handed down its decision on May 12, 2026. The trial court terminated the mother's parental rights and named the foster parents as joint managing conservators.Records from the Texas Fourteenth Court of Appeals show the mother appealed the decision, arguing mainly that the foster parents had no legal standing to bring the case in the first place.She argued that they did not meet the requirements of two sections of the Texas Family Code: 102.003(a)(9) and 102.003(a)(12). The provisions relate to situations where non-parents can bring proceedings regarding a child based on their care, possession or foster parent status.The mother also questioned whether the foster parents had complied with a new law concerning affidavits filed by nonparents seeking relief in parent-child relationship proceedings.Why the appeals court upheld the rulingIn considering the dispute, the Texas Fourteenth Court of Appeals reviewed Section 102.005 of the Texas Family Code, which provides a separate basis for persons to seek termination of parental rights in addition to an adoption petition.Under the version of the law in effect in 2022, when the foster parents filed the petition, an adult could gain standing by demonstrating that she had actual possession and control of a child for at least two months in the three-month period before the petition was filed. The provision also recognized substantial prior contact with the child as another basis for standing.Liam had been living with the foster parents exclusively since April 2022, the appellate court noted. They also filed a petition and affidavit in support of their petition setting forth the length of care and relationship with the child.In this instance, the court found that the foster parents satisfied the relevant statutory requirements. It ruled that they were eligible under Section 102.005, and that was enough to give them standing, so it did not need to decide whether they were eligible under the other provisions the mother complained about.New affidavit requirement not applicableAnother substantial part of the Nov. 10 ruling was Section 102.0031, which became effective Sept. 1, 2025.The provision requires non-parents in certain proceedings to file an affidavit detailing how a denial of the relief requested could significantly impact a child’s physical health or emotional development.The mother argued that the foster parents’ failure to file an affidavit of service undermined their legal position.The Texas Fourteenth Court of Appeals, however, distinguished between general parental custody and visitation proceedings and cases specifically seeking termination of parental rights in conjunction with adoption.The court held that the latter category was separately regulated by Section 102.005, and that the legislature had not applied the new affidavit requirement to persons proving standing under that section. The decision was an issue of first impression for the appellate court.Appeals court affirms trial court rulingAfter reviewing the arguments and applicable legal provisions, the Texas Fourteenth Court of Appeals rejected the mother’s challenges and affirmed the lower court’s judgment.The Nov. 10 ruling affirms the termination of her parental rights and the appointment of the foster parents as joint managing conservators. The request for adoption was in the proceedings, but the appellate ruling itself did not issue a separate adoption order, it dealt with standing and affirmed the termination judgment.The ruling in the case, officially styled In the Interest of L.S., a Child, clarifies how Texas law handles foster parents seeking standing in termination and adoption proceedings.Image Courtesy: istockYou use AI every day. articles.title: US, UK see sharp fall in international student enrolments amid visa curbs: Survey
articles.summary: A recent survey reveals a sharp decline in international student enrolments in the US and UK, highlighting the impact of stringent visa policies and attracting students towards Asia and Europe.
articles.body: Universities in the United States and the United Kingdom are facing a decline in international undergraduate enrolments as students increasingly consider destinations in Asia and continental Europe, according to a global survey of higher education institutions.The US recorded a 13% fall in international undergraduate numbers, while the UK saw a 19% decline between October and August compared with the same period a year earlier. The findings are based on a survey of 437 universities across 63 countries conducted by Studyportals, NAFSA and Oxford Test of English.Canada and Australia also reported weaker demand, while institutions across Asia and continental Europe recorded stronger growth in international student enrolments.International students are an important source of income for universities, as they generally pay higher tuition fees than domestic students. Their contributions help institutions meet the costs of teaching and research, making overseas recruitment a significant part of higher education funding.The survey identified visa restrictions and government policies as the biggest obstacles to attracting international students. Delays in processing applications, stricter screening procedures and changes to post-study work opportunities have led some prospective students to postpone or abandon their plans to study abroad.US universities expressed the greatest concern about future recruitment, with more than a third of institutions expecting international enrolments to fall further in the coming years.The decline in demand for American universities comes amid tighter immigration scrutiny under President Donald Trump. His administration has expanded social media checks for international students, revoked thousands of visas and introduced stricter rules governing how long foreign students can remain in the country.The survey was conducted before the November 3 midterm elections, in which Democrats won control of both chambers of Congress. However, the president retains executive authority over visa policies.The UK has also introduced tighter rules for international students as successive governments attempt to bring down immigration levels. Most overseas students are now restricted from bringing dependents, while the government has plans to reduce the period graduates can remain in the country to work or look for employment.Dr Fanta Aw, executive director and CEO of NAFSA, said the findings highlighted the influence of government policies on students' decisions about where to pursue higher education and future careers."These survey results affirm what we've observed before: national policies matter to international students making major decisions about where to study, conduct research, or start a career," Aw said.You use AI every day. articles.title: After back-to-back failures, Isro successfully tests modified PSLV 3rd stage
articles.summary: BENGALURU: In an important step towards restoring the reliability of its workhorse Polar Satellite Launch Vehicle (PSLV), Isro Thursday said it
articles.body: BENGALURU: In an important step towards restoring the reliability of its workhorse Polar Satellite Launch Vehicle (PSLV), Isro Thursday said it successfully conducted a ground static test of the rocket’s modified third stage (PS3) at the Satish Dhawan Space Centre (SDSC) in Sriharikota.The test, conducted on Thursday, follows two consecutive PSLV mission failures in which anomalies were observed in the rocket’s third stage. Isro said it had comprehensively reviewed the stage’s design margins, raw material acceptance criteria, assembly procedures and quality checks before introducing modifications to strengthen the system.Isro said the modified PS3 solid motor incorporates improvements to its nozzle configuration and mechanical interfaces, along with additional redundancy in its sealing systems. The space agency has also revised procedures for accepting raw materials, assembling the motor and conducting non-destructive tests (NDT) during integration and transportation.The mechanical interfaces have also been strengthened, with redundancy introduced in the sealing systems. Isro said the adequacy of design margins had been verified and updated non-destructive testing procedures had been implemented at different stages of integration and transportation.The modifications follow setbacks involving PSLV-C61/EOS-09 in May 2025 and PSLV-C62/EOS-N1 in Jan 2026. Both missions encountered problems during the third stage, raising concerns about the reliability of a launch vehicle that has been central to India’s satellite launch programme.On May 18, 2025, PSLV-C61, carrying the 1,696-kg EOS-09 Earth observation satellite, lifted off from Sriharikota. While the first two stages performed normally, Isro detected a fall in chamber pressure during the third-stage burn, preventing the rocket from completing its mission. A national-level committee was subsequently constituted to investigate the failure and recommend corrective measures.The second setback came on Jan 12, 2026, when PSLV-C62, carrying the EOS-N1 Earth observation satellite and 15 co-passenger payloads, encountered an anomaly towards the end of its third stage. The vehicle experienced disturbances in its roll rates, followed by a deviation in its flight path, and could not place the satellites in their intended orbits.While both failures involved the third stage, the specific circumstances reported were different. The latest modifications, Isro said, followed a comprehensive review of the PS3 configuration and were aimed at improving its design margins and manufacturing and quality-control processes.The space agency said the performance of the modified solid motor and its subsystems would now be assessed through a detailed analysis of the test data. Further tests are planned based on the findings.The PSLV, a four-stage launch vehicle, has been a mainstay of India's space programme, undertaking missions ranging from Chandrayaan-1 and the Mars Orbiter Mission to Aditya-L1. Its return to dependable flight operations is important not only for Isro's own missions but also for India's commercial satellite launch commitments.Get the latest India News and Live updates. articles.summary: Gaurav Chopra, the 19-year-old Texas man charged with the triple murders of his parents and grandmother at their family home in Alton earlier this year,
articles.body: Gaurav Chopra, the 19-year-old Texas man charged with the triple murders of his parents and grandmother at their family home in Alton earlier this year, may not face the death penalty as reports said state prosecutors are unlikely to seek the death penalty against him. The Hidalgo County District Attorney’s Office confirmed the decision on November 10, but they did not explain why they are against capital punishment for Chopra.The charges stem from the June 16 incident in which Chopra allegedly shot and killed his father, 56-year-old Sweeta Ram, his mother, 46-year-old Kamlesh Rani, and his grandmother, 73-year-old Minder Kaur.Chopra pleaded not guilty to the charges.According to previous reports, Alton police officers responded to a home in the 3700 block of Roosevelt Avenue after receiving a 911 call from a man who reported that his brother, identified as Chopra, had shot their family members and fled the scene.Authorities said Chopra also fired at his brother but missed.He was arrested after a police pursuit ended in a crash near the intersection of 4 Mile Line and Glasscock roads. Two people travelling in the vehicle he struck were hospitalised following the collision.Sweeta Ram was alive when officers arrived. He was taken to a local hospital where he died.During a July 6 hearing, a crime scene specialist with the Hidalgo County Sheriff's Office testified that investigators recovered $12,666 in cash and a weapon from the vehicle Chopra was driving. According to Hidalgo County jail records, Chopra remained in custody. He was being held without bond on the capital murder charge, while bond for the attempted capital murder and evading arrest charges was set at $500,000.Authorities have not disclosed a possible motive for the killings."UTRGV is aware that a suspect in an off-campus criminal investigation has been identified as a current student. The university is cooperating with law enforcement as appropriate. Because this is an active criminal investigation, questions about the case should be directed to the investigating agency," the University of Texas Rio Grande Valley issued a statement to ValleyCentral when the bone-chilling triple murders were reported and Chopra was revealed to be a student of the university.You use AI every day. articles.title: A Mississippi landlord claimed a couple running a youth sports nonprofit owed $99,468 after occupying property without a signed lease; a November 10 appeals court revived the suit without deciding whether they owed rent
articles.summary: A Mississippi landlord can continue pursuing a $99,468 claim against a couple accused of failing to pay rent and carry out repairs at a property in
articles.body: A Mississippi landlord can continue pursuing a $99,468 claim against a couple accused of failing to pay rent and carry out repairs at a property in Jackson. An appeals court has overturned the dismissal of the lawsuit, finding that the lower court went beyond what it had been asked to decide.The ruling delivered on November 10, does not establish that Thomas and Birdia Leonard owe the money. Instead, the Mississippi Court of Appeals has sent the dispute back to the county court, where the landlord's claims will be examined further.According to the ruling, the case involves Amrut Patel and his company, Venture Investors LLC, which had leased a property at 5124 North State Street in Jackson to the Leonards. The disagreement arose over the terms of their rental arrangement, including payments and renovation work that the landlord said the couple had agreed to undertake.Venture maintained that the couple had taken possession of the premises after paying $4,000 but later failed to meet their financial and repair obligations. The Leonards disputed the claim, pointing out that they had never signed the proposed lease agreement.The disagreement eventually reached the courts, with Venture seeking compensation for alleged unpaid rent and unfinished work. Although the county court dismissed the landlord's complaint, the appeals court found that the dismissal itself was not legally justified.Couple took possession after initial $4,000 paymentThe rental arrangement began with a letter of intent (LOI) setting out the proposed terms. The document required the Leonards to make an initial payment of $4,000. It also outlined a monthly rent of $3,500 for the later months of the proposed 36-month arrangement.The couple was also expected to spend $8,468 on renovations to the property. Birdia and Thomas Leonard signed the letter, but Venture Investors did not.There was another important condition in the document. It stated that the proposed arrangement would have no binding effect until both the landlord and tenants had signed a formal lease. That agreement was never completed, and the copy later submitted to the court also carried neither party's signature.Venture said the couple nevertheless accepted the arrangement by making the initial payment and moving into the property. The company alleged that they subsequently failed to pay the agreed rent and complete the renovation work.The Leonards offered a different account of what happened after they took possession. In their response to the lawsuit, they acknowledged that an oral agreement existed but maintained that their $4,000 payment was a down payment.They also said they had tried to secure permission to repair the buildings. However, the City of Jackson did not issue the required permits because of code violations at the property.Landlord calculated losses at $99,468Venture claimed that the couple's occupation of the property continued until November 2018. According to the company, they were supposed to start paying monthly rent of $3,500 from July 2018 and continue until August 2020.The landlord alleged that these payments were never made. It also said the promised renovation work remained incomplete and that the property had deteriorated because the couple failed to maintain it.Based on these allegations, Venture put its claimed losses at $91,000 in unpaid rent and $8,468 for repairs that were not completed. The combined amount came to $99,468.The company approached the county court seeking summary judgment, which would have allowed it to obtain a decision without a full trial.It submitted several records to support its position. These included the letter of intent, the unsigned lease, a $4,000 cashier's cheque and receipts relating to work at the premises.Some receipts covered grass cutting, fence work and machinery rental. The company also produced documents connected to Pro-Way Youth Sports, the non-profit organisation started by the Leonards.Venture pointed to the organisation's registration records, business address and other documents to support its claim that the couple intended to use the premises for youth sports activities. Birdia Leonard's deposition also confirmed that she and Thomas had started the organisation together.The company argued that the couple had failed to fulfil their commitments and that the documents were sufficient to establish the breach.County court dismissed landlord's complaintThe Leonards opposed the request for summary judgment. Their main argument was that the parties had never signed a formal lease, meaning there was no binding written rental agreement.They also maintained that the absence of a signed agreement had prevented them from getting an opportunity to carry out the proposed repairs.The county court found that the documents presented by Venture did not establish a valid contract. It said the papers contained missing elements and inconsistencies that prevented them from being treated together as a binding agreement.The court also found insufficient evidence to support recovery under the competing unjust enrichment claims. It consequently dismissed Venture's complaint.Venture challenged that decision before the Hinds County Circuit Court. However, the circuit court upheld the county court's order, prompting the company to approach the appeals court.Appeals court identifies problem with dismissalThe appeals court examined whether Venture had established enough evidence to obtain summary judgment on the basis of an oral agreement.It found that the company had relied heavily on the letter of intent to explain the alleged rental terms. But the document itself clearly stated that it was non-binding until a formal lease was signed by both parties.The judges also noted that Venture had not produced testimony or an affidavit explaining what the landlord and tenants had actually agreed to verbally.The fact that the Leonards had acknowledged an oral agreement did not, by itself, establish that they had accepted all the rental conditions claimed by Venture.The appeals court said a party seeking summary judgment over an alleged oral contract must provide some evidence of the actual verbal understanding. Venture had not done so. Its claim that the proposed terms could be inferred from the letter of intent was not enough.However, this did not mean the county court could dismiss the entire lawsuit. The judges drew a distinction between rejecting Venture's request for summary judgment and deciding the case in favour of the Leonards. The couple had not filed their own request for summary judgment. They had only asked the court to reject the landlord's application and allow the dispute to proceed.The appeals court said the county court should have stopped after finding that Venture had failed to establish grounds for summary judgment. It should not have dismissed the complaint when the defendants had not asked for that relief.The judges also referred to an earlier Mississippi ruling that cautioned against granting summary judgment to a party that had not sought it.The court therefore reversed the circuit court's decision and the county court's dismissal order. It remanded the matter to the county court for further proceedings on Venture's breach of contract claims.You use AI every day. Now get your AI Quotient. Take the AIQ test.

articles.title: A 17-year-old Australian boy vanished in dense bushland without his phone, food or water on November 6; six days later, police spotted his tackle box from a helicopter and found him alive beside a creek
articles.summary: For six days, a vast stretch of unforgiving Australian wilderness became the setting for a desperate search and a mother's agonising wait.
articles.body: For six days, a vast stretch of unforgiving Australian wilderness became the setting for a desperate search and a mother's agonising wait. Separated from his camping companion and without a mobile phone, adequate food or drinking water, 17-year-old Australian boy had to find a way to survive freezing nights, difficult terrain and the uncertainty of being lost. As hundreds of rescuers searched the dense Victorian bushland, hope remained that the teenager would be found alive. On Thursday, November 12, that hope turned into relief when a police helicopter spotted his fishing tackle box, leading rescuers to the exhausted teenager resting beside a creek.A camping trip takes an unexpected turnAccording to ABC News, the boy named William disappeared on November 6 after being dropped off near a campsite at Walhalla East, approximately 180 kilometres east of Melbourne, Victoria. He had been camping with a teenage friend, marking his first independent camping experience. A teen left the campsite to get more camping gear from the drop-off. But he went the wrong way and never returned.The Guardian reported that his friend initially searched for him but could not locate him. William had left his mobile phone, food and water behind, making his disappearance particularly concerning.His family later confirmed that the teenager has Level 2 autism, a condition that can involve substantial support needs and difficulties with communication and changes to familiar routines, according to information cited by AP News.Six days of survival in the wildernessWith no phone to contact anyone, William had to navigate the challenging landscape on his own. According to 9 News, he survived by drinking water from a nearby creek and rationing a family-sized packet of chicken-flavoured potato chips, which lasted him approximately two days. He also managed to keep himself warm during the cold nights using two towels and a pillow. Despite the difficult conditions, he continued moving through the rugged terrain for several days while trying to find his way back, the report stated.ABC News reported that William's mother, Elizabeth Barkley, later explained that her son had initially taken shelter beneath bushes after losing his way. When he resumed walking the following day, he lost his footing and fell down a steep riverbed embankment.His fall left him with scratches and sore legs. Unable to navigate the steep surroundings, he eventually remained near the creek for the final two days, resting and waiting for help.Huge search operationWilliam's disappearance triggered a major search operation involving police officers, emergency personnel and local volunteers.According to ABC News, more than 80 volunteers participated in the search each day, while the wider operation involved hundreds of people over six days. Specialist teams, including police divers, the Dog Squad and helicopter crews, were deployed to cover the challenging landscape.9 News reported that the search also involved the Public Order Response Team, Mounted Branch, Search and Rescue Squad and Victoria Police's Missing Persons Squad. Divers were brought in to examine nearby waterways as authorities expanded their efforts.The Guardian reported that investigators had also appealed to hunters, campers and landowners for information that could help establish the teenager's whereabouts. Despite the extensive ground search, the dense vegetation and steep terrain made certain sections extremely difficult to access.A tackle box leads rescuers to WilliamThe breakthrough came on Thursday morning when Victoria Police's Air Wing spotted a fishing tackle box in the bushland, approximately two kilometres from the location where William had last been seen. According to AP News, the helicopter crew subsequently located the teenager lying on a flat rock beside a creek. He had been resting in the dry riverbed, surrounded by rugged wilderness.ABC News reported that William was sleeping when the helicopter approached. After waking up to the sound, he waved at the aircraft and celebrated his discovery by pumping his fist. Rescuers were winched down to reach him before bringing him to safety. His pillow, lunch box and a small table were also found nearby. The teenager was shirtless and visibly sunburned, with cuts and scratches on his legs. However, he remained conscious, responsive and in relatively good spirits, the report added.An emotional reunion with his motherOne of the most moving moments of the rescue was William's reunion with his mother, who had remained hopeful throughout the search.According to The Guardian, footage captured the teenager smiling as he saw Elizabeth approaching the police helicopter before embracing her. And ABC News reported that Barkley was overwhelmed with relief and described the reunion as an almost unreal experience. She had been at the police staging area in Cowwarr when she received the news that her son had been found. The teenager later communicated his feelings about the rescue through his mother, expressing happiness and relief at being located after experiencing fear, loneliness, hunger and thirst.Recovery after the ordealWilliam was taken to Latrobe Regional Hospital for medical monitoring. According to ABC News, hospital chief executive Don McRae described his condition as remarkable given the circumstances and noted that his physical fitness had helped him endure the ordeal. AP News also reported that police considered him to be in good spirits and mostly in good health. His mother thanked the hundreds of volunteers and emergency workers who had dedicated their time to finding him.Image Courtesy: Victoria Police via APYou use AI every day. Now get your AI Quotient. articles.title: In 1975, Elvis Presley handed his customized guitar to a stunned fan during a concert; nearly 41 years later, it sold for $334,000
articles.summary: Discover how Elvis Presley shocked a fan by gifting his customized Gibson Dove guitar during a 1975 concert, which later sold for an astonishing $334,000 at Julien's Auctions in 2016.
articles.body: According to Julien’s Auctions, Elvis Presley was partway through “See See Rider” in Asheville, North Carolina, when he stopped what he was doing and gave the guitar in his hands to a fan. The fan, Mike Harris, had come for the show and left with a customised Gibson Dove that had already been seen by a worldwide television audience. Harris kept the guitar for nearly 41 years. In May 2016, Julien’s Auctions sold it in New York for $334,000, including the buyer’s premium. Accounts offer on exactly what Presley said, as he handed it over, but the fan walked out with an instrument that had been central to the singer's stage act for several years.Vernon Presley commissioned the guitar from Guitar City in 1969 and Elvis received it in 1971The guitar was originally intended as a gift from Elvis’s father. According to Julien’s Auctions, Vernon Presley visited the shop called Guitar City that was situated close to Graceland in Memphis in 1969, in order to purchase a Gibson Dove guitar for his son. It was Guitar City that applied the ebony finish, while Randy Wood of Gruhn Guitar created the “Elvis Presley” inlay on the fretboard of the guitar. The guitar was given to Elvis Presley in 1971. According to Julien’s Auctions, the guitar’s black finish was meant to symbolise Elvis earning a black belt in karate and the guitar had a Kenpo Karate sticker.The guitar was used by Elvis Presley on stage during 1971-1973, including his concert “Aloha from Hawaii” Julien’s Auctions reports that Presley was often pictured holding the guitar during 1971 to 1973 years. The highlight of this period was Aloha from Hawaii, the concert broadcast worldwide by satellite on January 14, 1973. Artnet described the performance as the first concert broadcast globally by satellite. The Asheville show, where Presley gave the guitar away, came on the last night of the three-night run in 1975. According to Julien’s Auctions, Presley was playing “See See Rider” when he gave the guitar to Mike, who was shocked to receive the present. Just Collecting dates the concert to July 24, 1975, and the Elvis Presley Music website page for that show lists the same date.It is unknown what exact words Elvis used. As Julien’s Auctions points out, different accounts differ and according to Artnet, Elvis is supposed to have said something like “Someday, it will help you out.” There is another report saying that he advised Mike to keep the guitar as he would need it someday because of its value. News of the gift spread fast. According to Artnet, Harris was recorded leaving the venue along with the police, as noted by Julien’s Auctions. Harris then held the guitar from July 1975 until May 2026, just under 41 years.The guitar sold for $334,000 at Julien’s Auctions on May 21, 2016Gibson Dove from Elvis Presley‘s estate was auctioned at Julien’s Auctions' ' Music Icon’ auction on 21st May, 2016 in New York, as reported by the BBC at the Hard Rock Cafe. The highest bid for the item was $270,000 and the total hammer price was $334,000, which includes the buyer’s premium. According to Artnet, the pre-sale estimate for the item was $300,000, so the $270,000 hammer price fell short of it and only the buyer’s premium pushed the final price to $334,000. articles.title: Around 1971, George Harrison offered an Apple engineer a Rickenbacker, calling it “a great rhythm player”; 43 years later, it sold for $657,000
articles.summary: Discover the fascinating story behind George Harrison's gifted Rickenbacker guitar to engineer George Peckham, which later sold for an astonishing $657,000 at auction. Learn about its history and significance in the music world.
articles.body: George Peckham, a cutting engineer at Apple, had borrowed a guitar from George Harrison for a Top of the Pops appearance with his band, The Fourmost. When he went to return it, Harrison asked whether he would like a guitar of his own and held out a 1962 Rickenbacker he rated highly for rhythm playing, calling it “a great rhythm player”. Peckham accepted on one condition that he would never alter it. According to The Associated Press, the guitar was later sold at the Julien’s Auctions Music Icons event at the Hard Rock Cafe in New York in May 2014. About 43 years after the gift, it sold for $657,000, above the top of its estimate.Harrison bought the 1962 Rickenbacker 425 in Mount Vernon, IllinoisAccording to the pre-auction statement of Julien‘s Auctions, Harrison bought the guitar, with serial number BH 439, in 1963, in Mount Vernon, Illinois, where he spent two weeks visiting his sister, Louise. It came in Fireglo red initially, but Harrison had it repainted black, like John Lennon‘s identical Rickenbacker. According to Julien’s Auctions, he used the guitar while recording the Beatles’ “I Want to Hold Your Hand’ at Abbey Road Studios. Harrison can be seen in a photo taken backstage during a concert in Scotland in October 1963 with the guitar.George Peckham was an Apple cutting engineer who used to play guitar in LiverpoolChristie's lot notes describe Peckham as a person with a long-standing relationship with Harrison and Apple. They stated that he was a chief cutting engineer of Apple in the late 1960s and 1970s and began his career as a guitarist in Liverpool. These notes also revealed that in 1971, he was closely associated with Harrison and even travelled to New York to master All Things Must Pass.Harrison offered the guitar after Peckham returned a borrowed one around 1971According to Julien’s Auctions, Peckham borrowed a guitar from Harrison for performance on Top of the Pops as a rhythm guitarist in The Fourmost band. When Peckham returned it, Harrison inquired if he wanted to keep a guitar and introduced him to the Rickenbacker guitar, stating that it was a great rhythm player. The guitar is said to have been gifted to Peckham only under the condition that it would never be altered. Julien’s Auctions notes mention this same story along with the fact that the guitar had good action. While Julien’s Auctions dates this gift to the late 1960s or early 1970s, Christie's notes claim that Peckham and Harrison were working closely together in 1971. These same notes mention two letters from Harrison’s office from Olivia Harrison and Caroline Foxwell, his assistant.A letter dating to the 1980s from Christie’s notes adds an interesting point about the guitar. According to it, Noddy Holder of Slade found Peckham’s guitar left in the corner and unable to bear the thought of a Beatles’ guitar being carried around without a case, gave Peckham one of his guitars. The 2014 sale was not the guitar’s first trip to auction. It had been offered at Christie’s in 1999, which makes Julien’s Auctions its second auction appearance. The guitar was auctioned as part of Julien’s Auctions’ Music Icons, Legends and Rebels event, held on May 17-18, 2014, at the Hard Rock Cafe in New York. According to The Associated Press, it was sold for $657,000, while Julien’s Auctions had estimated it to be sold at $400,000-$600,000 before the sale. Art Daily reported that the Music Icons, Legends and Rebels auction raised over $3.5 million, a figure that NBC Chicago also attributed to the auction house. articles.title: In the 1940s, Babe Ruth gave his “Called Shot” jersey to a golfing friend; about 80 years later, it sold for $24.12 million
articles.summary: Discover the incredible story behind Babe Ruth's iconic 'Called Shot' jersey, which sold for a record-breaking $24.12 million at Heritage Auctions. Learn about its history, provenance, and significance in sports memorabilia.
articles.body: Around 1940, Babe Ruth gave one of his old Yankees road jerseys to a golfing friend in Florida. Nothing about the gesture suggested it was a big deal. It was a grey flannel shirt from a career that had already produced plenty of them. Decades later, that jersey was identified as the one Ruth wore for his famous “called shot” home run in Game 3 of the 1932 World Series. Early on Sunday, August 25, 2024, it sold at Heritage Auctions in Dallas for $24.12 million, a record for any sports collectible sold at auction.Ruth hit his famous home run in the fifth inning of Game 3 The story begins at the Chicago Cubs’ Wrigley Field. According to the National Baseball Hall of Fame, 49,986 people attended this game and the Cubs’ players had been provoking Babe Ruth ever since the World Series started. It was said that in the fifth inning, according to the Associated Press, he had thrown a gesture from the plate and had hit a home run against Charlie Root at deep centre field. According to the Society for American Baseball Research, that day Root had given away two home runs each to Ruth and Lou Gehrig and the Yankees had beaten them 7-5. The Associated Press states that they also beat the Cubs the following day.Whether Ruth called the shot is still disputedAccording to NPR, Ruth himself endorsed many accounts of the event in the past and he even alleged that he had called his shot. According to the Hall of Fame, there was only one contemporary account that directly mentioned it, although others referred to the act of pointing. Cubs first baseman Charlie Grimm, Pat Pieper, the Wrigley Field announcer and Gehrig supported Ruth’s account. There is room for debate on the visual evidence as well. According to the Hall of Fame, two home videos by Matt Miller Kandle Sr. and Herold Warp capture Ruth in high spirits. Artnet notes that the video does not have any sound, while AP claims that, according to Michael Gibbons from Babe Ruth Birthplace and Museum, it is uncertain whether Ruth was pointing at the pitcher, centre field, or the Cubs players.Ruth gave the jersey to a golfing friend in Florida around 1940According to Heritage Auctions, Ruth kept the jersey and presented it to his golfing friend from Florida sometime in the 1940s, as per the Associated Press. That is according to Heritage’s account of its provenance and the jersey remained with this family for many years. Artnet, citing Heritage, says the daughter of the owner sold it in the early 1990s for a six-figure sum to an early pioneer in sports auctions, who then promptly sold it to an anonymous collector. The jersey next appeared at auction in 2005, attributed to the called shot, fetching $940,000, per the Associated Press. The jersey has since been in private hands until it came to Heritage in 2024.Photo comparison linked the jersey to Game 3, but the identification was contestedThe authentication process became another topic of discussion. Artnet says the consignor from New Jersey contacted an authenticator in 2019, who did not provide any clear results of the examination. According to Artnet, MeiGray and PSA relied on photo comparison to link the jersey to Game 3, looking at details such as the button location, embroidered letters and a stain.According to NPR, Heritage said several third parties matched the jersey using three photos taken before and after the game, but one of those companies ruled before the auction that its photo matching could not confirm a match. So, Heritage and other authenticators analysed photos in order to connect the jersey to Game 3, but the identification process was not unambiguous.The jersey sold for $24.12 million after a bidding war of more than six hoursAccording to The AP, Heritage auctioned the jersey very early on Sunday, August 25, 2024, in Dallas, following a bidding contest that lasted more than six hours to an unknown buyer. NPR added that the amount paid was close to double the previous highest sale of sports memorabilia, which was a 1952 Topps Mickey Mantle baseball card sold at Heritage for $12.6 million in 2022. This is more expensive than the most expensive game-worn jersey, Michael Jordan's NBA Finals shirt in 1998, that was sold for $10.1 million in 2022. Chris Ivy, the Director of Sports at Heritage, called it the most important piece of American sports memorabilia ever auctioned, according to The AP. Artnet had him referring to it as essentially the Mona Lisa in a statement to ESPN.You use AI every day. Now get your AI Quotient. Take the AIQ test.

articles.title: Around 2004, Alberta’s Jerry Leussink began building a 317,000-gallon swimming pond; cleaning and maintaining it takes 15–20 hours a month, and refilling it after a full drain took over a month
articles.summary: Discover how Jerry Leussink transformed a farm dugout into a stunning 317,000-gallon swimming pond near Sundre, Alberta, with extensive maintenance and innovative solutions for keeping it clean.
articles.body: A Canadian man decided to build a perfect summer hangout spot for his family near Sundre, Alberta. A farm dugout became an unusually large private swimming retreat after Jerry and Marina Leussink transformed it. By 2017, the swimming pond was reported as a 90-by-70-foot feature that was capable of holding approximately 317,000 gallons of water and reaching a depth of around 14 feet. However, with the massive scale came a maintenance commitment. In an interview with FOX 13, Leussink estimated that cleaning and maintaining the pool took between 15 and 20 hours every month. He also shared that once, when he emptied the pond, it took him more than a month to refill it with water after proper cleaning.There is, however, an important distinction in the pond’s construction history. FOX 13 reported in July 2017 that the Leussinks had installed the pool in 2013, citing Wide Open Country. But a past interview published by The Western Producer in December 2011 records that Jerry dug up the original pond approximately seven years prior and installed a white liner after another three years. Therefore, the earlier account places the beginning of the project around 2004.From the farm pond to a family swimming retreatLeussink originally wanted a place his family could use for swimming during the summer. In the 2011 interview, he recalled having a pond but wanting to evolve that idea further. He reportedly rented his brother’s truck and excavated a dugout measuring approximately 110 by 90 feet on the farm near Sundre. Three years later, he pumped out the water and brought in a crew of around 10 people to install a heavy white plastic liner, which eventually trimmed the swimming area to a 90-by-70-foot feature. The intention of the plastic liner was to reduce weeds and mud while making the bottom of the pool easier to clean.The liner was reportedly stretched up the sides and was secured with large boulders and thousands of washed rocks placed around the perimeter. Leussink, along with his wife, Marina, slowly started adding other characteristics that made the pond feel like a recreational swimming area instead of a conventional farm dugout. Over the years, the family continued to add improvements, thus turning the surrounding property into a gathering place for friends and relatives.Algae and debris created a regular maintenance routineAlgae became the pond’s biggest maintenance challenge. In the 2012 report, FARM SHOW Magazine quoted Jerry, saying that material blowing into the water provided food for algae. Furthermore, leaves, pine needles, insects and other debris accumulated at the bottom of the pond and around its liner. As per his estimate, around 15 to 20 hours a month were spent on cleaning and maintaining the pond, rather than spending that entire period exclusively removing algae.The cleaning routine reportedly included a combination of manual work with homemade equipment and water treatment. A long-handled brush helped remove the brown film that usually collected on the liner, while a swimming pool net was used to collect the insects and leaves. In addition to this, he also built a vacuum using approximately 60 feet of hose, PVC pipe and a two-inch pump to remove the accumulated debris from the bottom.Another part of the routine included water treatment. Jerry used chlorine, algaecides and swimming-pool chemicals to manage the water, while pond dye helped limit sunlight exposure and reduce conditions that encourage algae growth. This combination of routines allowed him to keep the lined pond usable for swimming.What a full drain meantThe scale of the pond became more apparent when Leussink decided to empty it for a thorough cleaning. The FARM SHOW Magazine reported that he pumped the pond dry after using it for a couple of years. Removing the accumulated algae allowed him to clean the pond before refilling it. However, restoring the water level proved to be a challenging process. His well pump took more than a month to refill it back to its estimated capacity of 317,000 gallons of water.Despite the upkeep, the pond turned into a regular destination for family gatherings. The property reportedly included camping areas, a horseshoe pit, a sandbox and space for outdoor activities. Notably, the water used for swimming in the summers could also serve as a skating rink in winter when conditions allowed. In the 2011 interview, Leussink estimated spending around $18,000 for the project, excluding his own labour.You use AI every day. Now get your AI Quotient. Take the AIQ test.

articles.title: A Texas businessman said he bought a home in 2015 with a partner's help while abroad, but she died and her children inherited it; an appeals court rejected his ownership challenge despite a $287,000 bank transfer
articles.summary: A Texas businessman who claimed he paid for a property that later passed to his deceased business partner's children has lost his ownership challenge in
articles.body: A Texas businessman who claimed he paid for a property that later passed to his deceased business partner's children has lost his ownership challenge in an appeals court. This was despite presenting evidence of a $287,000 bank transfer that he said was used to buy the property. The Fifth Court of Appeals of Texas at Dallas upheld a lower court's decision. It found that Kyle Harmon and his co-appellant, Gina Maria Ottavio, had failed to prove that a serious legal error was made in the probate orders. Those orders included a residential property in Plano, Texas, as part of the estate of Karrie Ellen Peterson.Harmon testified that while working overseas in 2015, he asked Peterson, his business partner in Hair Color Studios.com, LLC, to help him purchase the property. However, the warranty deed dated June 2015 named a different company, H.C.S LLC, as the property buyer. The deed was never officially recorded in the county's property records, although a copy was given to the local appraisal district. In August 2021, Karrie Peterson died without leaving a will. After her death, a corrected document was filed in August 2022. It changed the name of the buyer on the 2015 deed from H.C.S LLC to Hair Color Studios.com, LLC. At the same time, Peterson's children, Hunter Scott Brasher and Sarah Nichols, were recognised as her legal heirs and appointed as co-independent administrators of her estate.Failure to prove a resulting trust claimThe case, which was reported on the legal website Justia, focused on whether the $287,000 Harmon transferred shortly after the property purchase created what is known as a "resulting trust". This is a legal arrangement in which one person holds property for another because that other person provided the money used to buy it. In its written opinion, the Court of Appeals explained that proving this type of trust requires strong evidence. The judges found that Harmon's evidence was not enough to meet this legal standard.According to the official court decision, the "only evidence of Harmon's payment of the purchase price is his own testimony." Although the businessman referred to bank records to support his claim, the court explained that "that exhibit shows only that Harmon transferred approximately $287,000 to an unidentified money-market account a week after the deed to Hair Color Studios.com LLC." The judges also pointed out that the records "does not establish to whom Harmon sent the money, for what purpose he did so, or that Peterson received, and used, Harmon's money to buy the Property." The court explained that the trial judge was responsible for deciding whether witnesses were believable. The judge could have accepted all of Harmon's testimony, rejected it entirely or decided that his statements alone were not enough to meet the high legal standard required to prove a resulting trust.Disputed deeds and legal authorityThe ownership dispute also involved different property deeds and business entities. A 2019 deed appeared to transfer the property from H.C.S. LLC to Peterson personally. Harmon argued that this transfer was not authorised because Peterson did not have the legal power to act on behalf of the company. However, the Court of Appeals pointed out that "the only testimony of Peterson's purported lack of authority is Harmon's testimony, which... the trial court was free to disregard or credit but find to be insufficient." The appeals court also noted that the case records did not clearly explain the exact ownership and management structure of the business. This left open the possibility that Peterson had the authority to make the transfer because she was a majority owner of the company named on the deed. "As the proponents of the bill-of-review, Appellants bore the burden to conclusively prove Peterson's lack of authority to enter into the 2019 transaction," the court ruled. "Because they did not do so, they failed to establish that the 2019 deed was invalid."Finality in probate judgmentsHarmon and Ottavio had filed what is known as a "statutory bill of review" to challenge an earlier probate court decision that awarded the property to Peterson's children. This type of legal challenge is limited and examined very carefully. Courts generally want to ensure that final judgments remain settled. The appeals court explained that to receive a new review of a probate court order or judgment, "a party must specifically allege and prove substantial error by the trial court." The person making the challenge must prove this at trial using a preponderance of the evidence. This means showing that their version of events is more likely to be true than not. The Court of Appeals concluded that the trial judge had not abused their discretion by finding that Harmon and Ottavio failed to meet the high legal standard needed to show a serious error in the final probate decision. The judges concluded that "undisputed evidence and conclusive evidence are not the same." They rejected the businessman's only appeal argument. As a result, the lower court's decision remains in place, and the Plano property will continue to be treated as part of the estate of the late Karrie Peterson.You use AI every day. articles.title: A Mississippi woman's home caught fire in 2023 and her insurer estimated $440,092 in structural damage; after she sought full coverage and filed 1,385 pages of evidence, a federal appeals court rejected her claims
articles.summary: A federal appeals court has rejected a Mississippi homeowner's latest attempt to receive full insurance coverage after a fire damaged her property.
articles.body: A federal appeals court has rejected a Mississippi homeowner's latest attempt to receive full insurance coverage after a fire damaged her property. This happened despite her submitting a large collection of evidence, which totalled 1,385 pages, to support her claim. The U.S. Court of Appeals for the Fifth Circuit rejected the homeowner's arguments on November 10, 2026, according to the court records. The decision ends a legal dispute that began several years ago. The case started after a major fire damaged the woman's home in 2023. After the fire, the homeowner's insurance company carried out an inspection to work out how much damage the property had suffered. Following this assessment, the insurer prepared an official estimate that placed the cost of structural damage at $440,092.The nature of the valuation disputeAlthough the insurance company's estimate was substantial, the homeowner was unhappy with the amount. She argued that the $440,092 estimate did not cover the full extent of the damage or the actual costs needed to repair and restore her home. The main disagreement was over the difference between the insurer's estimate for structural damage and the homeowner's demand for "full coverage" under her insurance policy. When an insurance company and a policyholder disagree over a claim, providing proof of the losses is an important part of the process. The policyholder must give the insurer clear, detailed and reliable evidence showing the damage and the amount of money needed to cover it. The Mississippi homeowner disagreed with the insurer's estimate and began collecting a large amount of material to challenge its decision and support her demand for full payment.Volume of evidence and the initial court actionIn an effort to challenge the insurance company's estimate and receive the full coverage she believed she was entitled to, the homeowner gathered a huge amount of paperwork and other evidence. According to the case records, her submission eventually reached 1,385 pages. The documents were meant to show the full extent of the damage and explain the costs of repairs, replacements or rebuilding. The homeowner wanted to show why the insurer's original estimate was not enough to cover her losses. Fire damage claims involving large amounts of money can require several types of evidence. These may include building and repair estimates, lists of damaged personal belongings, photographs and expert reports about the condition and safety of the building. The size of the homeowner's submission showed how complicated the dispute had become. It also reflected the effort she had made to prove that the original $440,092 estimate was not enough to settle her insurance claim.The disagreement eventually reached the federal court system. The available case information does not provide full details about why the first court rejected her claims. However, the fact that she appealed to the U.S. Court of Appeals for the Fifth Circuit shows that an earlier court had already ruled against her. An appeal asks a higher court to review a previous decision. The appeals court mainly looks at whether the lower court made legal mistakes or incorrectly applied the law. It does not normally repeat the entire trial or simply consider new facts.Federal appeals court final decisionAfter the appeal was filed, the U.S. Court of Appeals for the Fifth Circuit reviewed the dispute between the Mississippi homeowner and her insurance company. The main purpose of this review was to decide whether the lower court had followed the law and handled the case correctly. Federal appeals courts examine the legal reasoning behind an earlier decision. They also review the evidence that was properly considered during the original court proceedings. On November 10, 2026, the appeals court issued its final decision in case 25-60625, according to the official court records. After reviewing the arguments, the judges were not convinced by the homeowner's appeal. The decision effectively upheld the earlier dismissal of her demand for full insurance coverage.The Fifth Circuit's ruling confirms the lower court's decision and rejects the homeowner's continued attempt to receive more compensation for the 2023 fire. For the Mississippi homeowner, the decision effectively ends her efforts to obtain higher insurance coverage through this federal appeals process. Her appeal was rejected despite the 1,385 pages of evidence she had submitted. The outcome also highlights the importance of meeting the legal requirements when challenging insurance decisions in federal court. A large amount of paperwork alone does not guarantee a successful claim. It also shows how important appeals court decisions can be, as they can bring a lengthy legal dispute to an end.You use AI every day. Now get your AI Quotient. Take the AIQ test.

articles.title: 'Foreign troops in Ukraine unacceptable': Putin's blunt message during meeting with Trump's envoys
articles.summary: Russian President Vladimir Putin on Thursday warned that any foreign troops deployed in Ukraine would be considered \"legitimate targets\", saying their
articles.body: Russian President Vladimir Putin on Thursday warned that any foreign troops deployed in Ukraine would be considered "legitimate targets", saying their presence would threaten Russia's security.Putin made the remarks during a meeting with US special envoy Steve Witkoff and Trump's son-in-law Jared Kushner at the Kremlin in Moscow.According to Reuters, Putin said European countries wanted to deploy troops in Ukraine after a peace agreement and added that Moscow would consider them legitimate targets."We said from the very beginning that the presence of any foreign troops on Ukrainian territory is absolutely unacceptable for us, because we believe it threatens the security of the Russian Federation," Putin said during the televised meeting, according to the Kremlin remarks reported by Reuters.The meeting was attended by US President Donald Trump's special envoy Steve Witkoff and his son-in-law Jared Kushner, alongside Putin's foreign policy aide Yuri Ushakov, defence minister Andrei Belousov and presidential envoy Kirill Dmitriev.Referring to the possibility of European forces entering Ukraine after a peace agreement, Putin said, "That after peace is concluded, they will immediately bring troops into Ukraine. What does that mean? We have already said that for us it is a legitimate target, meaning the war will immediately resume."He also said Russia wanted Washington to work with European countries on the wider security arrangements. "I would like the United States to work with Europe so that the Europeans could decide whether they want peace or war," Putin said.Putin further stressed that Moscow wanted a lasting settlement rather than a temporary pause in fighting, saying peace in Ukraine must be "eternal".Kushner, during the meeting, told Putin that Russia and Ukraine had made progress in negotiations but remained divided over how to implement a peace agreement. He said the two sides had "agreed on many of the principles, but are still apart on some of the way to accomplish" peace, according to the Associated Press.Kushner also raised the issue of European participation in future negotiations, telling Putin that European countries wanted to be involved in discussions on Ukraine's future security arrangements. Washington has been seeking a broader negotiating framework involving European governments alongside Russia, Ukraine and the US.Witkoff, meanwhile, highlighted progress made during the recent US-mediated negotiations in Abu Dhabi, particularly the agreement on a major prisoner-of-war exchange between Russia and Ukraine. He described the development as an encouraging sign in the diplomatic process.Before entering the Kremlin, Witkoff was asked whether the progress in negotiations meant peace was closer. "I hope so," he replied, according to Reuters.The meeting followed two days of trilateral negotiations involving Russia, Ukraine and the United States in Abu Dhabi on November 10 and 11. The talks resulted in an agreement on a prisoner exchange but failed to produce a breakthrough on territorial demands and post-war security arrangements.You use AI every day. articles.title: In 2022, a Tennessee deputy hunting a 34-year-old suspect stopped a 64-year-old disabled veteran with long purple hair and tased him, fracturing his skull; four years on, the county has agreed to pay him $1 million
articles.summary: A disabled US Air Force veteran who suffered a fractured skull after being Tasered by a Tennessee deputy will receive $1 million from Knox County.
articles.body: A disabled US Air Force veteran who suffered a fractured skull after being Tasered by a Tennessee deputy will receive $1 million from Knox County. The settlement comes four years after the incident, in which the deputy was searching for a 34-year-old man but stopped Brian Eugene Hux, who was 64 at the time.Hux was on Edington Road in South Knox County on October 10, 2022, when Deputy Randall Williams approached him. Williams was looking for a hospital patient who had escaped police custody. However, the information circulated among officers about the person they were seeking differed from Hux's appearance, according to the lawsuit.According to WVLT News, the alert described a man aged 34, standing six feet tall and having brown hair. Hux, meanwhile, was 64, measured 5 feet 9 inches and had long purple hair. He was also a 100% disabled Air Force veteran.The encounter ended with Hux being struck by a Taser in the back of his head. He fell face-first onto the road. Medical records referred to in the lawsuit documented a fractured skull and bleeding in his brain. The injuries were described as permanent, and Hux now requires round-the-clock care at an assisted living facility.The incident led to a civil rights lawsuit against Williams and Knox County, filed a year later. Hux initially demanded $3 million in damages. The county has now agreed to settle the case for $1 million, his lawyer Lance Baker confirmed to WVLT News.Body camera footage became part of the lawsuitThe lawsuit challenged the deputy's decision to stop Hux, arguing that he bore little resemblance to the person described in the police alert. It also disputed the circumstances in which Williams used his Taser.According to the legal filing, footage from the deputy's body camera showed Hux walking away before the confrontation escalated. The lawsuit alleged that he started running only after Williams charged towards him. Williams then fired his Taser, hitting Hux in the back of the head.Hux fell onto the asphalt, sustaining injuries that left him with lasting medical problems. The records cited in the case included evidence of the skull fracture and brain bleed. He now stays in a 24-hour assisted care facility.The lawsuit questioned whether Williams had sufficient grounds to stop Hux in the first place. It also challenged the argument that an outstanding warrant against Hux justified the deputy's actions.Court ruling allowed civil rights case to proceedIn July, a federal appeals court backed an earlier decision refusing to grant Williams qualified immunity. The ruling meant the deputy could not use this legal protection to have the claims against him dismissed at that stage.The appeals court identified three issues in its decision. It pointed to the absence of reasonable suspicion for the initial stop, the allegation that Williams had caused Hux to flee, and the constitutional rights of a person who has an outstanding warrant.Williams's legal team had argued that Hux's outstanding warrant meant the stop did not violate his civil rights. The appeals court did not accept that position.The decision was significant for Hux's case because it allowed the lawsuit to continue towards trial. Knox County had contested the claims for more than three years before the parties reached an agreement.Lawyer says settlement followed lengthy legal fightBaker confirmed on November 9 that Knox County had agreed to pay Hux $1 million. The amount is lower than the $3 million he had originally sought through the lawsuit.In a statement issued on Hux's behalf, Baker said the county had initially refused to offer his client any payment. He credited the eventual settlement to the prolonged legal battle and the federal appeals court's decision, which he said supported the merits of Hux's claims.Baker also said Hux had remained committed to pursuing the case despite the lengthy proceedings. The lawyer said his team had continued to challenge the county's position throughout the litigation.He added that Hux had stayed determined to see the case through and that the settlement would allow him to move forward.You use AI every day. articles.title: In 2001, Mark Wahlberg and his brother founded a charity for disadvantaged children; 25 years later, it has raised and distributed nearly $20 million, building community spaces and sending thousands to summer camp
articles.summary: A safe place to spend time after school, an opportunity to attend summer camp or access to creative facilities can make a lasting difference in a child's
articles.body: A safe place to spend time after school, an opportunity to attend summer camp or access to creative facilities can make a lasting difference in a child's life. For young people growing up in financially disadvantaged communities, however, such opportunities are not always within reach. Actor Mark Wahlberg and his brother Jim sought to address this gap by establishing a charitable organisation focused on helping children overcome financial barriers and access opportunities that could shape their futures.Founded in May 2001, the Mark Wahlberg Youth Foundation has raised and distributed nearly $20 million to youth organisations across the United States over the past 25 years. According to the foundation's official mission page, its work includes funding youth programmes, building basketball courts, recording studios and art spaces, and sending thousands of children to summer camp. Its public grant records, compiled from IRS Form 990 filings and published by Philanthropy.org, also show millions of dollars distributed to organisations supporting young people.The Foundation began with a mission to remove financial barriersThe Mark Wahlberg Youth Foundation was established by Mark and Jim Wahlberg in May 2001. Its central objective is to ensure that financial circumstances do not prevent children from pursuing their goals or reaching their potential.The foundation's origins are connected to Mark's own childhood experiences. Growing up in a family of nine children, he spent much of his free time at a local Boys and Girls Club. He has credited the organisation with providing a positive and supportive environment that helped shape his life.That experience influenced the foundation's approach to philanthropy. Rather than operating only its own facilities, it raises and distributes money to youth service organisations and enrichment programmes that already work with children in different communities. Its mission also focuses on improving the quality of life of young people in inner-city neighbourhoods through partnerships with other organisations.Nearly $20 million distributed to youth organisationsThe foundation reports that it has raised and distributed nearly $20 million to organisations across the country. Its support covers several areas, including education, recreation, health, after-school activities and opportunities for children from financially disadvantaged backgrounds. Its grant records provide a closer look at this work. According to Philanthropy.org's compilation of IRS filings, the foundation awarded approximately $4.4 million through 130 grants to 70 organisations between 2020 and 2024.The Boys and Girls Clubs of Dorchester in Massachusetts was the largest recipient during this period, receiving approximately $1.3 million through five grants. Other beneficiaries included the Gavin Foundation, which received $330,000, and Moving Mountains, which received $185,000. The foundation's support also reached organisations working in education, recreation, health and community development. These grants allow local organisations to continue programmes and provide services to children and families who might otherwise struggle to access them.Summer camps and community spaces create opportunitiesOne of the foundation's recurring initiatives is Camp Northbound, an annual summer camp programme for children from Boston neighbourhoods. The week-long experience takes participants to Maine, where they take part in sports, outdoor activities and traditional camp events.According to the foundation, thousands of children have benefited from its summer camp efforts over the years. Its 2024 tax filing, as reported by Philanthropy.org, recorded approximately $899,000 in programme expenses for youth support and summer camp activities. The programme includes opportunities for former campers to return as junior counsellors, giving them a chance to develop leadership skills.The foundation has also invested in physical spaces where children can learn, create and spend time in supportive environments. Its projects have included basketball courts, recording studios and art spaces in Boys and Girls Clubs and schools across the country. Another annual initiative is its holiday party for members of Boys and Girls Clubs throughout Massachusetts, where thousands of children receive gifts.Health awareness and education form part of its workBeyond recreation, the foundation supports programmes addressing serious challenges affecting young people and their families. Its initiatives have included work on substance abuse awareness through the film If Only, which aimed to encourage conversations about opioid abuse among young people and parents. It also partnered with the Drug Enforcement Administration and Walmart to organise youth summits focused on opioid awareness. Its 2024 tax filing also recorded support for health, medical and substance abuse programmes, alongside school support and after-school initiatives.Twenty-five years after its establishment, the Mark Wahlberg Youth Foundation continues to work through partnerships and grants to expand opportunities for children. Its nearly $20 million in reported fundraising and distributions reflects a long-running effort to make education, recreation, creative activities and supportive community spaces more accessible to young people.You use AI every day.
