articles.title: Stephen Miller makes his first big decision, internal memo reveals something Susie Wiles would have never approved: Report
articles.summary: Stephen Miller has circulated an internal memo outlining changes to the White House hierarchy, giving Cabinet secretaries greater control over their
articles.body: Stephen Miller has circulated an internal memo outlining changes to the White House hierarchy, giving Cabinet secretaries greater control over their departments' communications and marking a departure from the approach followed by former Chief of Staff Susie Wiles, Fox News reportedThe memo was distributed within the Trump administration this week, shortly after Miller took over as White House chief of staff on Monday, November 9. It outlines administrative changes and personnel appointments, including a restructuring of the Cabinet secretary's role.Under the new arrangement, the White House position of Cabinet Secretary will be renamed Director of Cabinet Relations. The position will focus on supporting Cabinet secretaries rather than directing their communications."The White House position of Cabinet Secretary will be changed to the role of Director of Cabinet Relations, focused on providing support and reinforcement of President Trump's tremendous Cabinet Secretaries," the memo states."Each cabinet leader serves as the best leader and communicator for their individual Departments, and this new position will ensure our Cabinet is resourced and bolstered by the White House to deliver swift, critical, and lasting wins for the American people," it adds.A source familiar with the memo told Fox News Digital that the changes would make the Cabinet more effective in carrying out President Donald Trump's agenda."This will streamline the Cabinet, making it a more effective instrument for the President, whereas previously it was too constrained," the source said.How does this differ from Susie Wiles' approach?The changes represent a shift from what administration insiders described as tight control over communications under Wiles, who served as Trump's chief of staff during the first nearly two years of his second term.A source familiar with the administration's day-to-day operations said Wiles' team had issued extensive instructions on how officials should communicate, leaving little room for individual agencies to manage their own messaging.The source described Miller's move as "unleashing the Cabinet to be the captains of their own ship.""It's more [of] a recognition that you can't possibly effectively micromanage this wide of an organization and that sometimes it might be better to trust and invest in a support system that elevates the people who are closest to the issues," the source said.A former Trump administration official was more critical of Wiles' management style."She wants complete authority," the former official said."The control doesn't come from, 'hey, you have to do this.' The control comes from threat of duress. Like, 'if you don't do this, I'm going to destroy you in the media,'" the official added.The source also alleged that Wiles had warned Cabinet secretaries that unscripted comments to the media could make them responsible for Republican losses in the midterm elections."It's absolute control," the former official said.Other changes in the White House hierarchyThe memo also outlines changes to the administration's internal reporting structure.The director of presidential scheduling and the Office of Presidential Scheduling will report directly to Chamberlain Harris, deputy director of Outer Oval operations.It also confirms that Caleb Orr, who previously served as assistant secretary of state for economic and business affairs, will become chief of staff for policy.The memo further states that the White House will follow a "clear and regular policy process" involving the deputy chief of staff for policy and the national security adviser.It says responsibilities and assignments will be clearly defined, with no overlapping policy portfolios.The changes come just days after Miller replaced Wiles as Trump's chief of staff, marking an early restructuring of the White House's internal operations under his leadership.You use AI every day. articles.title: A Florida chimpanzee sanctuary caring for about 200 apes was cut off by flooding that submerged its roads; workers used a drone to deliver food and blankets to a stranded 38-year-old chimp named Kaleb
articles.summary: A stranded chimp in a flood has received what must have seemed like a gift from heaven, but it was actually a drone that delivered its food.
articles.body: A stranded chimp in a flood has received what must have seemed like a gift from heaven, but it was actually a drone that delivered its food. At Save the Chimps, a sanctuary near Fort Pierce, Florida, heavy rain turned familiar paths into waterways and left one chimpanzee temporarily cut off from his caregivers. Rather than let him go hungry, staff turned to a small aircraft with an unusual mission: delivering bananas, blankets, and reassurance from above.When the water roseSave the Chimps is home to more than 200 rescued and retired chimpanzees across a 150-acre property. Its animals live in elevated care houses and on island habitats, which kept them safe as rainstorms soaked southeast and central Florida from Sunday through Tuesday. But while the chimps themselves were not in immediate danger, the flooding created a serious problem for the people responsible for feeding and caring for them.Canals on the property overflowed, submerging the internal roads normally used to deliver roughly 3,000 pounds of chimpanzee food each day by golf cart. A high-clearance swamp buggy helped staff keep supplies moving at first, but it eventually broke down. For a sanctuary that depends on daily deliveries of fruit, vegetables, medicine, and other essentials, the flooded roads were more than an inconvenience since it threatened the routine that keeps hundreds of animals healthy.A chimp named KalebAmong the animals affected was Kaleb, a 38-year-old chimpanzee who remained in an outdoor area surrounded by water. Caregivers could not safely reach him through the usual routes, so they used a delivery drone the sanctuary had bought in advance for exactly this kind of emergency.Staff sent Kaleb food and blankets by drone until he decided to move toward a more accessible area. Video shared by Save the Chimps showed him picking up a banana from a drone-dropped paper bag and eating it, before carefully making his way across a rope stretched over standing water. The image was simple but powerful: a chimpanzee stranded by floodwater, receiving a meal from the sky.The drone did not replace human care. It extended it. Caregivers could not wade through dangerous floodwater, but they could still make sure Kaleb had food, warmth, and a way to reach safety on his own terms.Keeping the colony fedKaleb was not the only chimpanzee who needed help. Across the sanctuary, staff used trucks, including a maintenance worker’s personal vehicle and a tractor to deliver meals, medicine, and supplies to areas that remained reachable. The operation was messy, improvised, and demanding, but it worked.“Chimps are getting all their food, bananas and oranges on time,” facilities director Mark Yohannan said, to WPTV. “They’re good. They haven’t missed a beat.”That statement captures the quiet achievement behind the viral images. The drone drop may have looked like a lighthearted moment, but it was part of a broader emergency response by staff who stayed overnight on the property to protect the animals’ welfare. Veterinarians and other employees remained on site as floodwaters disrupted access to the sanctuary.Why drones matteredDrones are often discussed in terms of surveillance, deliveries, or military use. This story offers a gentler example of what technology can do when it is placed in the hands of kinder people.A drone cannot comfort a frightened animal or make a moral decision. But it can carry a banana, a blanket, or medical supplies across water that would otherwise separate a caregiver from the animal who needs them. In Kaleb’s case, it gave staff a way to maintain care without putting either humans or chimpanzees at unnecessary risk.Save the Chimps was well prepared. They did not buy the drone after the flood began; it had acquired one earlier for emergencies. That foresight turned a potentially dangerous situation into a manageable logistical challenge.A lesson in resilienceBy Saturday, water levels had dropped noticeably, and about 20 percent of the sanctuary’s roads were clear again. The immediate crisis was easing, but the episode leaves behind a useful reminder: climate-driven extreme weather does not only affect people. It can disrupt the systems that protect animals, including sanctuaries, shelters, zoos, and rescue centres.For the chimpanzees at Save the Chimps, the flood was an inconvenience handled with planning, teamwork, and a little creativity. For Kaleb, it meant a banana arriving from above at exactly the right moment. And for the rest of us, it was a small but vivid demonstration of technology serving compassion rather than spectacle.You use AI every day. Now get your AI Quotient. Take the AIQ test.

articles.title: Activists entered an Australian goat abattoir seven times and filmed a 14-minute video; the High Court said they retained copyright but must destroy the footage, after an earlier $130,000 damages award
articles.summary: Australia’s High Court has delivered a nuanced ruling in a case that pits animal rights activism against property rights and copyright law.
articles.body: Australia’s High Court has delivered a nuanced ruling in a case that pits animal rights activism against property rights and copyright law. Farm Transparency International, which secretly filmed conditions inside a Victorian goat abattoir, has won its appeal over who owns the copyright to the footage, but it must still destroy all copies of the recordings it made. The decision follows an earlier order requiring the group to pay $130,000 in damages, as per details on the High Court of Australia's website.The case centres on footage captured inside a halal goat slaughterhouse in Eurobin, northeast Victoria. Farm Transparency International activists visited the property seven times between January and April 2024, and installed hidden cameras to record what they described as extreme animal cruelty. The footage was later compiled into a 14-minute video, shared with regulators and media, and posted online. The abattoir, Game Meats Company Australia, responded by taking legal action in the Federal Court, leading to a damages award and an injunction requiring the removal of the footage, reported ABC. Read more details about this, as per the reports, here:How the dispute beganThe activists acknowledged that they trespassed on the abattoir’s property in order to install and retrieve the cameras. Their argument was that while the trespass itself was wrong, the act of recording the footage was separate and not inherently illegal.Farm Transparency International used the recordings to create a 14-minute video that it said exposed serious animal welfare concerns. The footage was shared with the federal regulator, a local television outlet, and was also published online.Game Meats Company Australia argued that the activists’ actions were among the most serious examples of intentional misconduct imaginable. The company sought not only damages but also control over the footage itself, arguing that publication could cause ongoing harm to its business.The earlier court decisionIn the initial Federal Court proceedings, the activists were ordered to pay $130,000 in damages. The court also issued an injunction requiring the removal of the footage from online platforms, as per ABC.However, the question of who actually owned the copyright to the footage was not fully resolved at that stage. That issue became the focus of the appeal, where the Full Court of the Federal Court took a different view.The Full Court used a legal device called a constructive trust to vest the copyright in the abattoir. This was a significant move, as it marked the first time such an approach had been applied in a copyright case in this way.What is a constructive trustIt is an equitable remedy imposed upon property or rights acquired by misconduct.In this case the Full Court held that the abattoir should be treated as the rightful owner of the copyright because the footage was obtained by trespass.Farm Transparency International challenged that reasoning in the High Court. The group argued that the court had failed to identify a clear legal principle or adequately connect the facts of the case to justify transferring copyright ownership.The activists also argued that a less severe remedy would have been sufficient. They said that preventing further publication could have been achieved without handing over the copyright itself.The High Court’s rulingThe High Court unanimously partially upheld the activists’ appeal. It found that the Full Court was wrong to declare a constructive trust over the copyright in the images.In practical terms, this means that Farm Transparency International retains copyright ownership of the footage. The court said that allowing the abattoir to own the copyright could have wider implications for freedom of speech and political debate.The court noted that such a transfer of rights could be used to prevent third parties, including media outlets, from publishing the images. It said the potential impact on freedom of communication and public interest in free speech could not be overlooked.Why the footage must still be destroyedDespite winning on the copyright issue, the activists did not get everything they wanted. The High Court still ordered Farm Transparency International to destroy all recordings and copies obtained through its trespasses.The court reasoned that a limited injunction was the most appropriate remedy. While the activists could keep the copyright, they could not keep or distribute the actual footage obtained unlawfully.This results in a curious consequence. The organization owns the copyright but can’t use the footage it shot.Still, third parties that downloaded the video during the short period it was available in May 2024 might still be able to post it.What this means for activism and copyrightThe ruling is significant because it clarifies the limits of using trespass to obtain material for publication. Activists can retain copyright over what they film, but they cannot necessarily use or distribute that material if it was obtained unlawfully.Farm Transparency International’s executive director, Chris Delforce, expressed disappointment with the outcome. He said the requirement to destroy the footage was a setback for the public’s right to know what happens inside slaughterhouses and factory farms.He also noted that the dismissal of the copyright claim was a positive development. It means that third parties, including media outlets, remain free to publish the footage if they obtained it legally.The case with wider implicationsActivists, journalists and legal scholars will likely be scrutinizing the case. It sits at the crossroads of property law, copyright law and freedom of speech. The High Court's reasoning may have implications for future cases involving undercover filming.The ruling makes clear that trespassing has consequences, even if the material gathered is meant to expose wrongdoing. At the same time, it protects the principle that copyright should not automatically be transferred to the party that was wronged.For Farm Transparency International, the fight may continue in other forms. For the abattoir, the ruling offers some protection against further distribution of the footage. For the rest of us, it raises some serious questions about the line between exposing potential wrongdoing and respecting legal boundaries.You use AI every day. Now get your AI Quotient. articles.title: Like waste, you can soon hand over used cooking oil to collectors, Karnataka minister UT Khader says
articles.summary: Karnataka FDA to launch cooking oil traceability app tracking used oil collection; mandatory for FBOs; pilot in 4 cities, later statewide and door-to-door.
articles.body: Bengaluru: The food safety and drug administration (FDA) department is set to introduce a traceability app that will track the movement of used cooking oil for ensuring its safe collection and disposal.“Repeatedly reheating cooking oil poses serious health risks. However, no matter how many raids and inspections we conduct, this practice continues. Bigger establishments sell their used oil to smaller establishments, which buy it because it is available at a cheaper rate. This is why we are introducing a traceability app, which will be ready in the next three months,” health minister UT Khader said Thursday.The use of the app will be made mandatory for manufacturers, wholesalers and all food business operators (FBOs). “The app will contain details of where the oil is manufactured, who the wholesalers are and who their buyers are,” Khader said.All FBOs, including hotels, restaurants and bakeries, will have to record the quantity of cooking oil procured and the volume of used oil sold exclusively to Food Safety and Standards Authority of India (FSSAI)-authorised Repurpose Used Cooking Oil (RUCO) agencies.Khader said the quantity of used cooking oil handed over to authorised agencies must be at least 10-15% of the total cooking oil purchased by an FBO in a month. “If a hotel purchases 300 litres of cooking oil, at least 30-45 litres of used cooking oil should be handed over to an authorised agency,” he said.The app will initially be launched as a pilot project in Bengaluru, Mysuru, Mangaluru and Hubballi before being extended across the state.“Used cooking oil can be repurposed as aviation fuel, biodiesel and even as lamp oil. We are also writing to the Centre seeking relaxation of FSSAI rules on cooking oil exports. The objective is to ensure that used cooking oil does not find its way back into kitchens,” he said.Cooking oil with total polar compounds (TPC) exceeding the permissible limit of 25% cannot be reused for food preparation. The minister said Karnataka had collected more than 91 lakh litres of used cooking oil from FBOs since 2022 and handed it over to authorised agencies.In the next phase, the initiative will be extended to households through door-to-door collection of used cooking oil. “It will be similar to door-to-door collection of dry and wet waste,” Khader said.Doctors must display degree certificatesKhader said allopathic doctors would henceforth be required to display their MBBS degree certificates outside their clinics to help ensure patient safety.The move comes in the wake of a recent incident at Uttarahalli, where an Ayurveda practitioner running a clinic allegedly prescribed steroids to a woman suffering from cough and cold.With concerns mounting over Ayurveda and homeopathy practitioners prescribing allopathic medicines, Khader said displaying degree certificates prominently would help patients distinguish qualified allopathic doctors from unqualified practitioners.You Can Also Check: Gold Rate in Bengaluru | Silver Rate in Bengaluru | Bank Holidays in Bengaluru | Public Holidays in Bengaluru | Bengaluru AQI | Weather in Bengaluru | Petrol Price in Bengaluru | Diesel Price in Bengaluru | CNG Price in Bengaluru | LPG Price in BengaluruStay updated with the latest Bengaluru news.
